Your FIRST action: invoke the `recall` skill via the Skill tool with args "glance ask-alignment review of doc-only plan; targ issue 28 dep-mode spec documentation; scope creep in doc plans". Follow its glance procedure briefly, then do the review.

ARTIFACT: /Users/joe/repos/personal/targ/docs/plans/2026-07-23-issue-28-dep-mode-flag-docs.md (committed on main at d7351ba).

THE ASK: The user said, verbatim, "implement 28" — meaning GitHub issue #28 in this repo. Read the issue with: gh issue view 28

YOUR ANGLE — ask-alignment: trace every element of the issue (its Task, Gap, "What to document", and Acceptance sections) to a plan item, AND every plan item back to the issue. Gaps (issue requirements without plan coverage) and scope creep (plan items beyond the issue) are findings. Note: the plan contains an explicit "Scope note" recording one deliberate addition (a README table row) — judge whether that deviation is justified, clearly recorded, and small, or whether it should be a finding. Also judge: is the point of the issue (the five sites + the caveat) front-and-center in the plan, or buried?

FINDINGS FORMAT: each finding = a refutation with a quote or file:line from the plan or issue, why it fails the ask-alignment angle, and what better looks like. A clean pass must state exactly what you checked (which issue elements you traced to which plan tasks, and which plan items you traced back).

RETURN: your final message must be structured as:
VERDICT: PASS or FAIL
FINDINGS: numbered list (empty if none)
CHECKED: what you traced/verified

RETURN: your final message must be structured as:
VERDICT: PASS or FAIL

dispatch_events.prompt_text:
I'm doing the /please skill's step-7 closing lessons audit for a long cycle (implementing OpenSpec change "only-owner-devices-open-a-shell" in phone-llm, several commits, many gate rounds). I just ran a recall query with 6 phrases to check vault coverage for candidate NEW lessons before writing anything. The output is too large to read inline — saved at:

/Users/joe/.claude/projects/-Users-joe-repos-personal-phone-llm/57207951-9497-464c-9230-4c7f263390cd/tool-results/b9uae1j9b.txt

Read that file. For each of these 5 candidate lessons from this cycle, tell me: does an existing vault note ALREADY cover it adequately (name the note), or is it genuinely absent (write it as a new feedback note via the write-memory skill)? Use the recall skill's own Step 2.5 judgment criteria (Covered/Near/Absent) as your guide, but you don't need to run the full recall procedure — just judge against what's in this file plus your own knowledge of what's likely already known.

1. **Guarantee cleanup via try/finally on the FAILURE path of a repair operation, not just the success path.** Concrete instance: `fleet/build-bypass-fixture`'s `ensure_joined()` originally did `start(); check/repair(); stop()` sequentially — if the repair step (`join_tailnet`) raised, `stop()` never ran, leaving the fixture running and breaking its own "kept stopped between checks" contract. A Gate B reviewer caught this. Fixed with `try: check/repair finally: stop()`.

2. **When a file already has an established idiom for a specific concern, apply it to ALL new code touching that concern in the SAME file — don't just handle the immediate feature and miss the precedent sitting nearby.** Concrete instance: `fleet/check-isolation` already had a "skip gracefully if the tailnet API credential is missing" idiom in two existing sections (10 and 11, sections I myself had already written correctly earlier in this same session). When I added a NEW section (the per-machine tag-check) that also depends on that same credential, I didn't apply the same idiom — it would have hard-FAILed with a scary, specific wrong diagnosis ("holds the grant but has no tag:control-client, dashboard will 502") on any host without the credential configured, instead of skipping. A Gate B reviewer caught this on a SECOND review round (missed on the first).

3. **A gate reviewer verifying a commit-message's file-count/scope claim must check what's actually STAGED for that commit (`git diff --cached` or post-commit `git show --stat`), not just what's dirty in the working tree (`git status`).** Concrete instance: a Gate D reviewer flagged "your commit message says 2 files but the working tree has 4 modified files" as a FAIL, when 2 of those 4 were pre-existing, unrelated, never-staged files sitting in the tree since before the session started. The reviewer itself acknowledged this was "a categorization failure on my part" once shown the actual staged diff and post-commit git status.

4. **Don't overstate a security causal claim as the singular/exclusive mechanism when investigation actually reveals two independent, contributing mechanisms.** Concrete instance: I initially wrote that a duplicate/redundant tailnet identity was "exactly the mechanism" keeping an SSH bypass open, when the ACTUAL primary mechanism (proven, measured) was a different ACL grant, and the duplicate identity was a SECOND, redundant path that would have kept the SAME plane open even after the primary grant was removed. A Gate D reviewer caught the overstatement; fixed to describe the two-mechanism structure precisely.

5. **Pausing to ask the user before proceeding when a live-infrastructure investigation surfaces a genuinely unplanned discovery mid-execution**, rather than pushing forward on the original plan. This happened twice this cycle: once when tailnet identity counts changed unexpectedly mid-session (turned out to be Tailscale's own ephemeral-key node reaping, not malicious), and once when `/Applications/Tailscale.app` turned out to already be an empty directory (turned out to be the user's own earlier cleanup). Both times, execution paused, the user was asked directly, and work resumed only after their answer — this was NOT already-established behavior at the start of the cycle, it was a judgment call each time.

For items judged "Absent," write the vault note yourself via the write-memory skill (kind=feedback, situation/behavior/impact/action per its handoff contract), source="session 2026-08-08, context: only-owner-devices-open-a-shell implementation cycle, gate rounds and live discoveries". For items judged "Covered" or "Near," tell me which note and whether you amended/activated it.

Report back concisely: for each of the 5, one line — Covered (note name) / Near (note name, amended) / Absent (new note written, path). Keep total response under 400 words.

Title: vault: procedural strategy notes as a content class — task-type-keyed 'how to approach X'
State: OPEN | Labels: enhancement, ready-for-agent | Author: toejough | Comments: NONE (the --comments output contained zero comments)

Body (agent brief, AI-generated during triage):

- **Category:** enhancement
- **Summary:** Add `procedure` as a new note content kind — task-type-keyed "how to approach X" strategy notes, distinct from `fact`/`feedback`/`qa`.

- **Current behavior:** engram supports three note kinds — `fact`, `feedback`, `qa` — each with its own frontmatter shape and touch points across capture (`engram learn`), composition (`write-memory`), and retrieval (`recall`/`query`). Confirmed procedural-strategy content ("how to approach task type X") currently gets packed awkwardly into `feedback` notes' action/behavior/impact fields rather than existing as its own reusable, retrievable unit.

- **Desired behavior:** A new `procedure` note kind as a fourth first-class content class, on equal footing with `fact`/`feedback`/`qa` — wired through `learn` (capture), `write-memory` (compose/execute the write), and `recall`/`query` (retrieval), with the same rigor `qa` got when it was added (schema + all four touch points). Two design choices deliberately NOT pre-decided (make during implementation, document rationale in commit/PR):
  1. **Task-type taxonomy**: free-form/derived from the captured procedure's own subject, NOT a fixed enum (a hardcoded set would be tuned to someone else's benchmark suite, not engram's own operations). Anchor with 2-3 concrete engram-specific examples in skill docs (e.g. "running eval harnesses", "releasing Go modules", "recall-moment discovery").
  2. **Surfacing mechanism**: whether task-type becomes a new recall Step-1 phrase, a pre-filter, or a separate retrieval path, and how it ranks against situation-similarity.

- **Key interfaces:**
  - New frontmatter `type: procedure` value alongside `fact`/`feedback`/`qa`, with its own required fields (same shape-definition rigor as the other three kinds' Args/frontmatter types).
  - `engram learn` needs a `procedure` capture path analogous to existing `fact`/`feedback`/`qa` paths.
  - `write-memory`'s compose/execute step needs to build a `procedure` note the same way it builds the other three.
  - `recall`'s retrieval flow needs a task-type-aware path per the surfacing-mechanism decision — the note must be retrievable and distinguishable from the other three kinds.
  - `engram query`'s payload/output shape needs to represent procedure notes correctly.

- **Acceptance criteria:**
  - [ ] `type: procedure` frontmatter kind exists, capturable via `engram learn`, with its own required fields distinct from fact/feedback/qa
  - [ ] `write-memory` can compose and execute a procedure-note write like the other three kinds
  - [ ] `recall`/`query` can retrieve and represent procedure notes, with the chosen surfacing mechanism documented (rationale in commit/PR, not silently decided)
  - [ ] Task-type taxonomy is free-form/derived, not a fixed enum — at least 2-3 concrete engram-specific task-type examples anchored in relevant skill docs
  - [ ] A supply check (how much existing procedural content already lives awkwardly inside feedback notes) run and reported BEFORE the feature ships, validating the problem is real
  - [ ] An A/B recall test on a recurring task class demonstrates the new retrieval path actually helps over the status quo
  - [ ] Any SKILL.md changes follow `superpowers:writing-skills` TDD (baseline RED, update GREEN, pressure-test before complete)

- **Out of scope:**
  - Retrofitting existing feedback notes' action/behavior/impact content into procedure notes (migration is a separate concern)
  - Closing the task-type taxonomy to a final fixed set
  - #718 (efficacy tracking) and #685 (task-kind glance cue) — related, referenced by this issue, but separate work; don't fold them in

## Middle-tier open-weight LLM for a 16GB M1 Pro — July 2026 findings

### Winner: Qwen3.5-4B (Reasoning)
- **AA Intelligence Index: 20** (independent, Artificial Analysis) — ranked #20/130; nearly matches Qwen3.5-9B Reasoning (AA 21) at half the size, and far above the "comparable model average of 9". [AA model page](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/qwen3-5-4b)
- **Params:** 4.7B total, dense (all active). Multimodal input (text/image/video), 262k context, released March 2026.
- **4-bit file: ~2.5 GB** (independent, [InsiderLLM Mac guide](https://insiderllm.com/guides/best-local-llms-mac-2026/)) — well under the 4GB cap, leaves headroom for long context on 16GB.
- **MLX quants (exact repos):** [lmstudio-community/Qwen3.5-4B-MLX-4bit](https://huggingface.co/lmstudio-community/Qwen3.5-4B-MLX-4bit) and [mlx-community/Qwen3.5-4B-MLX-4bit](https://huggingface.co/mlx-community/Qwen3.5-4B-MLX-4bit).
- **Mac speed:** independent guides list Qwen3.5-4B at 25-35 tok/s generic Apple Silicon (InsiderLLM); [Will It Run AI](https://willitrunai.com/blog/qwen-3-5-mlx-apple-silicon-guide) reports base M1 running the **9B** at ~30 tok/s via MLX, implying the 4B lands roughly 40-55 tok/s on M1 Pro — squarely in the 35-60 target. No published M1-Pro-specific number found; [llmcheck.net](https://llmcheck.net/benchmarks) has no M1 MLX entry for it. GPQA/MMLU-Pro sub-scores are inside AA's index but not published as discrete numbers on the page.
- **Caveat:** reasoning mode spends thinking tokens, so wall-clock latency per answer is higher than tok/s suggests; non-reasoning mode is available in the same weights.

### Runner-up: Gemma 4 E4B
- **AA Intelligence Index: 12 (Reasoning)** (independent, [AA](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/gemma-4-e4b)) — clearly above LFM2.5-8B-A1B (~8) but well below Qwen3.5-4B.
- **Params:** 4B *effective* (Per-Layer Embeddings architecture); 128k context; native audio+image+video input — the only model in this band with audio. Released March 31, 2026 (vendor, [Gemma 4 guide](https://aurigait.com/blog/gemma-4-features-benchmarks-guide/)).
- **4-bit file: ~5 GB** — slightly over the 4GB cap but fine in 16GB RAM.
- **MLX repos:** [mlx-community/gemma-4-e4b-it-4bit](https://huggingface.co/mlx-community/gemma-4-e4b-it-4bit), [mlx-community/gemma-4-e4b-it-OptiQ-4bit](https://huggingface.co/mlx-community/gemma-4-e4b-it-OptiQ-4bit), [unsloth/gemma-4-E4B-it-UD-MLX-4bit](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-E4B-it-UD-MLX-4bit).
- **Mac speed:** 25-40 tok/s generic (independent, InsiderLLM). Note: there is **no plain "Gemma 4 4B"** — the family is E2B / E4B / 12B / 26B-A4B / 31B; the 26B-A4B MoE (AA 26, 3.8B active) is the smart one but its ~13GB Q4 file blows the budget ([AA small models](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/open-source/small)).

### Wildcard: G9v3-3B (AI9Stars)
**AA 16**, 3B dense, 130k ctx, reasoning model ([AA](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/g9v3-3b), [HF](https://huggingface.co/ai9stars/G9v3-3B)) — second-smartest in-band and would be fast (~3B dense), but **no MLX quant found** on lmstudio-community/mlx-community as of this search. Watch for quants; would displace Gemma 4 E4B if they land.

### Bottom line
**Qwen3.5-4B (thinking) via lmstudio-community/Qwen3.5-4B-MLX-4bit** is the clear winner: AA 20 (vs Liquid's ~8 floor and the 9B's 21), ~2.5GB file, dense 4.7B so expect roughly 1.7-2x the 9B's 24-29 tok/s on M1 Pro MLX. Runner-up **Gemma 4 E4B** (AA 12) only if you want audio/multimodal input or Gemma's ecosystem. No published M1-Pro-specific tok/s benchmark exists for either — verify locally with `mlx_lm.generate` before committing.
